title: Präsens — regelmäßige Verben
summary: Regular present tense: drop -en, add personal endings.
explanation:
Most German verbs are regular in the present tense (Präsens). Take the stem (the infinitive minus -en) and add the personal ending.

The endings are -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en. German uses the present tense both for things happening now and for the near future.
tips: The wir and sie/Sie forms are identical to the infinitive.
German has no continuous tense: "ich spiele" means both "I play" and "I am playing".

title: Präsens — Schreibweise / Endungen
summary: Stems ending in -t/-d or -s/-ß need a spelling tweak.
explanation:
When a verb stem ends in -t or -d, an extra -e is inserted before the -st and -t endings so the word stays pronounceable: arbeiten → du arbeitest, er arbeitet.

When a stem already ends in an s-sound (-s, -ß, -z, -x), the du form drops the s of -st and just adds -t: heißen → du heißt, tanzen → du tanzt.
tips: Other -t/-d verbs: finden → du findest, antworten → du antwortest, reden → er redet.
For heißen/tanzen the du form (heißt, tanzt) looks like the er-form — that's correct.

title: sein (to be) — Präsens
summary: The most common irregular verb: bin, bist, ist …
explanation: sein (to be) is completely irregular and must be memorized. It is one of the most frequent verbs in German, used for descriptions, states, professions and locations.
tips: No article before a profession: "Ich bin Lehrer", not "ich bin ein Lehrer".
sein is also the helper verb for the Perfekt of movement verbs (ich bin gegangen).

title: haben (to have) — Präsens
summary: Irregular: habe, hast, hat, haben, habt, haben.
explanation: haben (to have) is irregular only in the du and er/sie/es forms, where the -b- drops out: du hast, er hat. It expresses possession and is also the most common helper verb for the Perfekt tense.
tips: German says "Hunger/Durst haben" (to have hunger/thirst) where English uses "to be".
haben is the helper for most Perfekt forms: "Ich habe gegessen".

title: Verben mit Vokalwechsel
summary: Stem-changing verbs change the vowel in du/er forms.
explanation:
Some strong verbs change their stem vowel, but only in the du and er/sie/es forms. The endings stay regular.

The common patterns are a → ä (fahren → du fährst), e → i (sprechen → du sprichst) and e → ie (lesen → du liest).
tips: The vowel change is only in du and er/sie/es — wir/ihr/sie keep the original vowel.
More examples: essen → du isst, nehmen → du nimmst, geben → du gibst, schlafen → du schläfst.

title: Modalverben
summary: können, müssen, wollen, dürfen, sollen, möchten + infinitive at the end.
explanation:
Modal verbs express ability, necessity, wishes and permission. They are irregular in the singular (often no -e in the ich form, and a vowel change).

A modal verb takes a second verb in the infinitive, which goes to the very END of the sentence (the "Satzklammer", or sentence bracket).

tables.caption: ich = er/sie/es (no ending); wir and sie/Sie = infinitive

examples.en: Would you like to drink a coffee?

tips: ich and er/sie/es have the SAME form (no -t): er kann, er muss.
The main verb stays as an infinitive at the end: "Ich will heute nicht arbeiten."
möchten is the polite "would like" — softer than wollen (want).

title: Trennbare Verben
summary: Separable verbs: the prefix splits off to the end of the sentence.
explanation:
Many verbs have a separable prefix (auf-, ein-, an-, mit-, ab-, aus-, zu-…). In a main clause in the present tense, the prefix separates and moves to the END of the sentence, while the conjugated stem stays in position 2.

Examples: aufstehen → ich stehe … auf; einkaufen → ich kaufe … ein.

examples.de: Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.
examples.en: I get up at seven o'clock.

tips: The stress is on the prefix: AUFstehen, EINkaufen.
With a modal verb the separable verb stays together at the end: "Ich muss früh aufstehen."
In the Perfekt the -ge- goes between prefix and stem: aufgestanden, eingekauft.
Regular separable verbs → ge-…-t (eingekauft); strong separable verbs → ge-…-en (angekommen).

title: Perfekt mit haben
summary: Past tense for speaking: haben + Partizip II at the end.
explanation:
The Perfekt is the normal spoken past tense. It is built with a helper verb (haben or sein) in position 2 plus the past participle (Partizip II) at the very end.

Most verbs use haben — especially verbs with an object and verbs that do not express movement.
tips: Use haben if there is a direct object or the verb has no movement.
The participle always goes to the end: "Ich habe gestern Deutsch gelernt."

title: Perfekt mit sein
summary: Movement and change-of-state verbs use sein as the helper.
explanation: Some verbs form the Perfekt with sein instead of haben. These are verbs of movement from A to B (gehen, fahren, kommen, fliegen) and verbs of change of state (aufstehen, einschlafen, werden), plus sein and bleiben themselves.

examples.de: Ich bin gestern ins Kino gegangen.
examples.en: I went to the cinema yesterday.

tips: Memory aids for sein: gehen, kommen, fahren, fliegen, laufen, reisen, aufstehen, einschlafen, werden, bleiben, sein.
bleiben and sein use sein even though there is no movement — just learn them as exceptions.

title: Partizip II — Bildung
summary: ge-…-t (regular), ge-…-en (strong), no ge- for -ieren / inseparable.
explanation:
The Partizip II (past participle) is needed for the Perfekt.

Regular (weak) verbs: ge- + stem + -t (machen → gemacht, spielen → gespielt).

Irregular (strong) verbs: ge- + (often changed) stem + -en (trinken → getrunken, sehen → gesehen).

No ge- prefix: verbs ending in -ieren (studieren → studiert) and inseparable-prefix verbs with be-, ver-, er- etc. (verstehen → verstanden, bezahlen → bezahlt).

tables.caption: Separable verbs — ge- between prefix and stem

tips: Separable verbs insert -ge- after the prefix: eingekauft, angerufen, ausgegangen.
Strong participles must be learned individually — there is no rule for the vowel change.

title: Imperativ
summary: Commands and requests: du-, ihr- and Sie-forms.
explanation:
The imperative gives commands, instructions and requests. There are three forms.

du: usually just the verb stem, no ending and no pronoun (komm!, geh!). Stem-changing e→i verbs keep the change (sprich!, lies!), but a→ä verbs do NOT (fahr!).

ihr: the normal ihr-form without the pronoun (kommt!, geht!).

Sie: verb + Sie, in that order (Kommen Sie!, Gehen Sie!).
tips: Add bitte to make a command polite: "Warte bitte!"
The Sie-form keeps the pronoun and looks like a question without the question mark.

title: Präteritum — haben und sein
summary: The simple past of haben (hatte) and sein (war) — used even in speech.
explanation: While most verbs use the Perfekt in spoken German, haben and sein are almost always used in their Präteritum (simple past) forms instead: ich hatte (I had), ich war (I was). These two forms are used far more often than "ich habe gehabt" or "ich bin gewesen".

examples.en: We had a lot of fun.

tips: ich and er/sie/es have the SAME form — no ending: war, hatte.
In spoken German, prefer "ich war" over "ich bin gewesen" and "ich hatte" over "ich habe gehabt".
Präteritum of modal verbs (konnte, musste, wollte…) also appears in speech, but at A1 focus on war/hatte.

title: Bestimmter Artikel — der/die/das
summary: The definite article shows gender: der (m), die (f), das (n).
explanation:
Every German noun has a gender: masculine (der), feminine (die) or neuter (das). The plural always uses die. The gender is grammatical and must be learned with each noun.

There are some hints, but they are only tendencies.

examples.en: The woman is reading the newspaper.

tips: Hints: -ung, -heit, -keit, -tion, -e are usually die; -er, -ling often der; -chen, -lein, -ment usually das.
Always learn a noun WITH its article — "der Tisch", not just "Tisch".

title: Unbestimmter Artikel — ein/eine
summary: a/an: ein (m/n), eine (f). No plural form.
explanation:
The indefinite article (ein/eine) corresponds to English "a/an". It is ein for masculine and neuter nouns and eine for feminine nouns.

There is no plural indefinite article — the plural simply has no article ("Ich habe Bücher").
tips: ein covers both masculine and neuter in the Nominativ — they only differ in the Akkusativ.
Drop the article entirely with professions: "Er ist Arzt."

title: Negativartikel — kein/keine
summary: kein is the negative of ein: "not a / no / not any".
explanation:
kein negates a noun that would otherwise take ein or no article at all. It means "no", "not a" or "not any". It takes the same endings as ein.

Use kein with nouns; use nicht to negate everything else (verbs, adjectives, etc.).

examples.en: That is not a good idea.

tips: Unlike ein, kein DOES have a plural form: keine.
Rule of thumb: if you could say ein or use no article in English, negate with kein.

title: Kasus: Nominativ, Akkusativ, Dativ
summary: The three A1 cases: subject (Nom), direct object (Akk), indirect object (Dat).
explanation:
German has three cases at A1 level. The Nominativ is the subject (wer/was?). The Akkusativ is the direct object (wen/was?). The Dativ is the indirect object (wem?) and follows certain prepositions.

In the Akkusativ only the masculine article changes (der→den). In the Dativ ALL genders change: der/das→dem, die→der, plural die→den (+‑n on the noun).

examples.de: Ich gebe dem Kind einen Ball.
examples.en: I give the child (Dat) a ball (Akk).

tips: Akkusativ: only masculine changes (der→den, ein→einen).
Dativ: all genders change — dem (m/n), der (f), den+‑n (pl).
Common Dativ contractions: in dem→im, an dem→am, zu dem→zum, zu der→zur, von dem→vom.

title: Pluralbildung
summary: Plurals form with -e, -er, -(e)n, -s or an umlaut.
explanation: German has several plural patterns and the article is always die in the plural. There is no single rule, so the plural should be learned with each noun, but these are the common patterns.

examples.en: The children are playing in the park.

tips: Feminine nouns very often take -(e)n in the plural.
-s is common with foreign/borrowed words (Autos, Hotels, Handys).

title: Großschreibung der Nomen
summary: All nouns are capitalized in German — always.
explanation:
In German EVERY noun is written with a capital letter, no matter where it stands in the sentence. This includes concrete things (der Tisch), people (die Frau) and abstract ideas (die Liebe).

The polite pronoun Sie (you) and its forms (Ihr, Ihnen) are also capitalized.

examples.de: Der Hund spielt mit dem Ball im Garten.
examples.en: The dog plays with the ball in the garden.

tips: If a word has an article (der/die/das/ein…), it is a noun and must be capitalized.
Capitalize formal Sie/Ihnen/Ihr, but not the informal du/ihr in normal text.

title: Personalpronomen — Nominativ
summary: ich, du, er, sie, es, wir, ihr, sie, Sie — the subject pronouns.
explanation: Personal pronouns in the Nominativ replace the subject of a sentence. Note that sie has three meanings: she (singular), they (plural) and — capitalized — Sie, the formal "you".
tips: du = one person you know well; ihr = several such people; Sie = polite, always capitalized.
Use er/sie/es to match the noun's gender, not the natural sex: "der Tisch → er".

title: Personalpronomen — Akkusativ
summary: mich, dich, ihn, sie, es, uns, euch, sie, Sie — object pronouns.
explanation: When a personal pronoun is the direct object, it takes the Akkusativ form. Only some forms change from the Nominativ; sie, es, Sie stay the same.
tips: er → ihn is the form learners forget most often.
Like the articles, only the masculine pronoun changes shape noticeably (er → ihn).

title: Personalpronomen — Dativ
summary: mir, dir, ihm, ihr, uns, euch, ihnen, Ihnen — indirect object pronouns.
explanation: When a personal pronoun is the indirect object (to/for whom), it takes the Dativ form. The Dativ is used after Dativ prepositions (mit, von, zu, bei, nach, aus) and with verbs that take a Dativ object (helfen, gefallen, gehören).
tips: uns and euch are the same in Akkusativ and Dativ.
ihm serves both masculine and neuter — just like dem.

title: Possessivartikel
summary: mein, dein, sein, ihr, unser, euer, ihr, Ihr — and they take ein-endings.
explanation:
Possessive articles show ownership (my, your, his…). Each personal pronoun has a matching possessive: ich → mein, du → dein, er → sein, sie → ihr, wir → unser, ihr → euer, sie → ihr, Sie → Ihr.

They take the SAME endings as ein/kein, so they agree with the gender, number and case of the noun that follows (not the owner).
tips: Be careful: sein = his, ihr = her — don't mix them up.
euer loses an e when an ending is added: euer → eure (eure Mutter).
Dativ endings are the same as ein/kein: -em (m/n), -er (f), -en (pl).

title: Verb an Position 2
summary: In a statement, the conjugated verb is always the second element.
explanation:
The core rule of German word order: in a normal statement, the conjugated verb stands in second position. Position 1 can be the subject, but also a time expression or another element — and then the subject moves after the verb (inversion).

"Position 2" means the second sentence element, not the second word.

examples.en: I am going to the cinema today.
Today I am going to the cinema.

tips: If you start with a time/place, the subject comes right AFTER the verb: "Morgen komme ich."
Never put two elements before the verb: not "Heute ich gehe…" but "Heute gehe ich…".

title: Ja/Nein-Fragen
summary: Yes/no questions start with the conjugated verb.
explanation: To ask a question that can be answered with ja or nein, put the conjugated verb in FIRST position, followed by the subject. No question word is used.
tips: Answer a negative question with doch to contradict it: "Hast du kein Auto?" — "Doch!"
No "do"-helper as in English: just move the verb to the front.

title: W-Fragen
summary: Question words (wer, was, wo…) + verb in second position.
explanation: W-questions ask for specific information. They begin with a question word (most start with W), and the conjugated verb comes right after it in second position, then the subject.
tips: woher = from where (origin), wohin = to where (destination) — don't confuse them.
The verb is always in position 2, right after the question word.

title: Konjunktionen: und, oder, aber, denn
summary: These connectors join clauses WITHOUT changing word order.
explanation: The coordinating conjunctions und (and), oder (or), aber (but) and denn (because/for) connect two main clauses. They sit between the clauses in "position 0" and do NOT affect the word order — the verb stays in second position in both parts.

examples.de: Ich lerne Deutsch und ich höre Musik.
examples.en: I learn German and I listen to music.

examples.de: Sie ist müde, aber sie arbeitet.
examples.en: She is tired, but she works.

examples.de: Ich bleibe zu Hause, denn ich bin krank.
examples.en: I am staying home, because I am sick.

tips: After und/oder/aber/denn the normal verb-second order continues unchanged.
denn (because) is different from weil — weil sends the verb to the end, denn does not.

title: Satzstellung: Zeit – Art – Ort
summary: Middle-field order at A1: time, then manner, then place.
explanation: When several pieces of information come in the middle of a sentence, German tends to order them as time (wann) → manner (wie) → place (wo/wohin). This is often summarized as TeKaMoLo (temporal, kausal, modal, lokal); at A1 just remember time before place.

examples.de: Ich fahre morgen mit dem Bus nach Hause.
examples.en: Tomorrow I am taking the bus home.

examples.de: Wir gehen heute Abend ins Restaurant.
examples.en: We are going to the restaurant this evening.

tips: A simple rule: time before place. "Ich komme um acht Uhr nach Hause."
You can move the time expression to position 1 for emphasis: "Morgen fahre ich…".

title: Präpositionen mit Akkusativ
summary: für, ohne, durch, gegen, um always take the Akkusativ.
explanation: A small group of prepositions is always followed by the Akkusativ case. Remember them as a fixed list. After them, masculine articles change: der → den, ein → einen.

examples.de: Das Geschenk ist für meinen Bruder.
examples.en: The present is for my brother.

tips: A common memory word: "FUDGO" — Für, Um, Durch, Gegen, Ohne.
um is also used for clock times: "um acht Uhr" (at eight o'clock).

title: Präpositionen mit Dativ
summary: mit, nach, bei, von, zu, aus always take the Dativ.
explanation:
Another fixed group of prepositions always takes the Dativ case. In the Dativ the articles become: der/das → dem, die → der, plural → den (+ -n on the noun).

At A1 it is enough to learn these as set phrases with the right article.

examples.en: We are going to the doctor.

tips: A memory phrase: "aus, bei, mit, nach, von, zu" — all Dativ.
Short forms: zu dem → zum, zu der → zur, von dem → vom, bei dem → beim.

title: Lokale Präpositionen — wo? wohin? woher?
summary: Location (wo? + Dativ), direction (wohin? + Akkusativ), origin (woher? + aus/von).
explanation:
The "Wechselpräpositionen" in, an, auf, and other location prepositions answer three different questions:

wo? (where? — static location) → Dativ: "Ich bin in der Schule."
wohin? (where to? — direction/movement) → Akkusativ: "Ich gehe in die Schule."
woher? (where from? — origin) → aus / von + Dativ: "Ich komme aus der Schule."

The same preposition (in, an, auf) switches case depending on whether there is movement to a destination or not.

tables.caption: in / an / auf — wo? (Dativ) vs wohin? (Akkusativ)
woher? — aus / von + Dativ
rows: aus der Schule, aus dem Haus

tables.caption: nach / zu / in — wohin?
rows: in die Schweiz, in den Park
zum Arzt, zur Schule, zu mir

examples.de: Wo bist du? — Ich bin im Park.
examples.en: Where are you? — I am in the park. (Dativ)

examples.de: Wohin gehst du? — Ich gehe in den Park.
examples.en: Where are you going? — I am going to the park. (Akkusativ)

examples.de: Woher kommst du? — Ich komme aus dem Park.
examples.en: Where are you coming from? — I am coming from the park. (Dativ)

tips: Static (wo?) = Dativ, movement (wohin?) = Akkusativ — this is the key rule for in/an/auf.
nach for cities and most countries (no article): nach Paris, nach Japan. in + Akk for countries with an article: in die Türkei, in die USA.
Contractions: in dem→im, in das→ins, an dem→am, an das→ans, zu dem→zum, zu der→zur.

title: Temporale Präpositionen
summary: um, am, im, von…bis, ab, seit, vor, nach — when things happen.
explanation: Temporal prepositions express when something happens. Most are followed by the Dativ case. At A1, learn these as fixed phrases with the right article.

rows: vor dem Essen, vor zwei Tagen

examples.de: Ich wohne seit drei Jahren in Berlin.
examples.en: I have been living in Berlin for three years.

tips: am for days and times of day (am Montag, am Morgen), im for months and seasons (im Mai, im Herbst), um for clock times (um 10 Uhr).
seit + Präsens = English present perfect: "Ich lerne seit einem Jahr Deutsch" = I have been learning German for a year.

title: Negation: nicht oder kein
summary: kein negates nouns; nicht negates everything else.
explanation:
German has two main words for "not".

Use kein to negate a noun that has ein or no article: "Ich habe ein Auto" → "Ich habe kein Auto".

Use nicht to negate everything else — verbs, adjectives, adverbs, and nouns that have a definite article or possessive: "Ich arbeite nicht", "Das ist nicht mein Auto".
tips: Quick test: if you could say "a/an" or no article in English, use kein.
kein takes ein-endings: kein, keine, keinen, keine (Pl.).

title: Die Position von nicht
summary: nicht goes at the end, but before the part it negates.
explanation:
For sentence negation (saying the whole action is not happening), nicht usually goes at the END of the sentence: "Ich verstehe das nicht."

But nicht stands directly BEFORE the specific element it negates — before an adjective, a place expression, or the second part of the verb (infinitive / participle / separable prefix).

examples.en: She does not live in Munich.

tips: With a modal verb, nicht comes before the infinitive: "Ich will nicht gehen."
nicht goes before the separable prefix / participle: "Ich rufe dich nicht an."

title: Wichtige Adverbien (A1)
summary: Frequency, time and place adverbs for everyday sentences.
explanation: Adverbs describe when, how often, or where something happens. Unlike adjectives, they never change form — no endings, no gender agreement. They typically go in the middle of the sentence (after the verb, before the place).

examples.en: I often go to the cinema.
The toilet is upstairs on the left.

tips: Adverbs of frequency often go right after the verb: "Ich trinke immer Kaffee."
Time adverbs can go to position 1 for emphasis: "Morgen fahre ich nach Hause."

title: Wichtige Verben mit Akkusativ
summary: Common A1 verbs that take a direct object in the Akkusativ case.
explanation: Most transitive verbs in German take a direct object in the Akkusativ. The Akkusativ answers the question "wen oder was?" (whom or what?). Only the masculine article changes: der/ein → den/einen.

examples.en: Do you know the man over there?
She is looking for her keys.

tips: Ask "wen oder was?" (whom or what?) to find the Akkusativ object.
Only the masculine article changes: einen Mann, but eine Frau, ein Kind.

title: Wichtige Verben mit Dativ
summary: A1 verbs that need a Dativ object — helfen, gefallen, gehören …
explanation: Some verbs take their object in the Dativ instead of the Akkusativ. These must be memorized. The Dativ answers "wem?" (to/for whom?). In the Dativ: der/ein → dem/einem (m/n), die/eine → der/einer (f), plural die → den (+‑n on the noun).
tips: gefallen works backwards compared to English: "Das Buch gefällt mir" = I like the book (lit. the book pleases me).
Ask "wem?" (to whom?) to find the Dativ object: "Ich helfe dir" → Wem helfe ich? → dir.

title: Ordinalzahlen
summary: erste, zweite, dritte … — ordinal numbers add -te / -ste and take adjective endings.
explanation:
Ordinal numbers say which position something is in (first, second, third …). In German, form them by adding -te to numbers 1–19 and -ste from 20 onward. Three are irregular: erste (1st), dritte (3rd), siebte (7th).

Ordinals behave like adjectives — they take the same endings depending on the article and case before them.

examples.en: Today is the third of May.
I live on the second floor.

examples.de: Nehmen Sie die erste Straße links.
examples.en: Take the first street on the left.

tips: 1–19 → stem + -te (except erste, dritte, siebte); from 20 → stem + -ste.
Dates use ordinals: "am dritten März" (on the third of March). Written: am 3. März (with a dot after the number).
After a definite article they take weak endings: der erste, die zweite, das dritte.

title: ab … bis vs von … bis
summary: ab = from … onward (open end); von … bis = from … to (both endpoints).
explanation:
Both express time spans, but they work differently.

von … bis names a START and an END: "von 9 bis 17 Uhr" (from 9 to 5). Both endpoints are stated.

ab names only a START with no fixed end — it means "from … onward": "ab morgen" (starting tomorrow, continuing). It often implies a permanent or indefinite change.

bis alone marks only the END: "bis Freitag" (until/by Friday).

examples.de: Der Laden ist von Montag bis Samstag geöffnet.
examples.en: The shop is open from Monday to Saturday.

examples.de: Ab morgen lerne ich jeden Tag Deutsch.
examples.en: Starting tomorrow I will study German every day.

examples.de: Ab Juli bin ich im Urlaub.
examples.en: From July onward I am on vacation.
Until when do you have time?

tips: von … bis = both endpoints are named (a defined window). ab = only the start, no end in sight.
bis can combine with other prepositions: "bis zum Bahnhof" (to the station), "bis nach Berlin" (as far as Berlin).
ab + Dativ: "ab dem ersten Januar", but in everyday speech often without article: "ab Januar".

title: Kontraktionen: ins, ans (Akkusativ)
summary: in das → ins, an das → ans — short forms for direction with neuter nouns.
explanation:
When the prepositions in or an are followed by das (neuter Akkusativ, indicating direction/movement), they contract:

in + das → ins: "Ich gehe ins Kino." (into the cinema)
an + das → ans: "Wir fahren ans Meer." (to the sea)

These are Akkusativ contractions (movement → wohin?). Compare with the Dativ contractions im (in + dem) and am (an + dem), which express static location (wo?).

examples.en: Are you coming to the pool?
The children run to the water.
We are driving into the center.
Write your name on the board.

tips: ins/ans = movement (wohin? → Akkusativ); im/am = location (wo? → Dativ).
The contraction is optional but very common in speech: "ins Kino" sounds more natural than "in das Kino".
These only work with das (neuter). For die/den there is no contraction: "in die Schule", "in den Park".

title: Unbestimmte Pronomen: alles, etwas, nichts
summary: alles = everything, etwas = something, nichts = nothing — always neuter singular.
explanation:
These three indefinite pronouns refer to things, not people. They are always treated as neuter singular and never change form.

alles = everything / all
etwas = something / some (also: a little / somewhat)
nichts = nothing / not anything

When followed by an adjective, the adjective takes a strong neuter ending (-es): etwas Neues (something new), nichts Besonderes (nothing special).

examples.en: Would you like to eat something?

tips: etwas is often shortened to was in casual speech: "Hast du was gehört?"
Adjectives after alles/etwas/nichts are capitalized (they act as nouns) and get the -es ending: etwas Schönes.
nichts is the pronoun (replaces a noun); nicht is the adverb (negates verbs/adjectives). Don't confuse them.

title: Frageartikel: welcher / welche / welches
summary: welcher = which? — takes der-like endings to match gender and case.
explanation:
welcher asks "which?" or "which one?" and works like a question article before a noun. Its endings follow the same pattern as der/die/das: -er (m), -e (f), -es (n), -e (pl.) in the Nominativ. In the Akkusativ, only the masculine changes to welchen.

Use welcher when there is a choice between several items.

examples.en: Which bus goes to the station?
In which city do you live?

tips: welcher follows the same pattern as dieser and der: -er (m), -e (f), -es (n), -e (pl.).
Only the masculine changes in the Akkusativ: welcher → welchen (like der → den).
welcher asks for a choice; was für ein asks about the type/kind: "Was für ein Auto hast du?" (What kind of car do you have?).

title: Demonstrativartikel: der / die / das (betont)
summary: Stressed der/die/das = that one / this one — used in speech instead of dieser.
explanation:
In everyday spoken German, the definite articles der, die, das are used as demonstratives when spoken with stress. They mean "this one" or "that one" and are far more common than dieser in conversation.

As demonstratives they can stand alone (without a noun) as pronouns: "Den nehme ich" (I'll take that one). Their forms are identical to the normal definite article in Nominativ and Akkusativ.

examples.de: Wie findest du das Kleid? — Das ist schön.
examples.en: How do you like the dress? — That one is nice.

tips: In speech, DER Mann (stressed) = dieser Mann. Germans strongly prefer the stressed article over dieser.
Standing alone without a noun, der/die/das works as a pronoun: "Die ist toll!" (That one is great!).
Don't confuse unstressed der (just the article) with stressed DER (the demonstrative) — only context and intonation distinguish them.

title: Perfekt vs. Präteritum
summary: When to use spoken-tense Perfekt vs. written-tense Präteritum.
explanation:
German has two past tenses that both translate as English simple past, but they're used in different situations, not different meanings.

Perfekt (haben/sein + Partizip II) is the everyday spoken past — used in conversation, phone calls, and informal writing (emails, chats) for almost every verb. Präteritum is the narrative past — used in written German (news, stories, formal reports) and, regardless of register, almost always for sein, haben, and the modal verbs (war, hatte, konnte, musste…), because their Präteritum forms are short and common even in speech.

examples.de: Gestern habe ich einen Film gesehen.

examples.en: Once upon a time there was a king. (written/narrative)
I was sick yesterday. (sein, spoken too)
We didn't have time. (haben, spoken too)

tips: In conversation, default to Perfekt — except for sein, haben, and modal verbs, where Präteritum sounds more natural even when speaking.
Both tenses describe the same past time; the choice is about register (spoken vs. written), not meaning.

title: Nebensätze: weil, dass, wenn
summary: Subordinate clauses send the conjugated verb to the end.
explanation:
A Nebensatz (subordinate clause) is introduced by a conjunction like weil (because), dass (that), or wenn (if/when) and cannot stand alone. Unlike main clauses, the conjugated verb moves to the very end of the clause.

weil gives a reason, dass introduces a reported statement or fact, and wenn introduces a condition or repeated/future event. The main clause and the Nebensatz are separated by a comma; if the Nebensatz comes first, the main clause's verb comes right after the comma (verb-second still holds for the whole sentence).

tables.caption: Word order shift
rows: Ich glaube, dass er morgen kommt.
Wenn es regnet, bleibe ich zu Hause.

examples.de: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank bin.
examples.en: I'm staying home because I'm sick.

examples.de: Sie sagt, dass sie keine Zeit hat.
examples.en: She says that she has no time.

examples.de: Wenn ich Geld habe, kaufe ich ein Auto.
examples.en: If/When I have money, I'll buy a car.

examples.de: Weil es kalt ist, trage ich eine Jacke.
examples.en: Because it's cold, I'm wearing a jacket.

tips: Verb-last is the single biggest signal that you're in a Nebensatz — always check the end of the clause, not just after the conjunction.
If the Nebensatz starts the sentence, the comma is immediately followed by the main clause's conjugated verb.

title: Relativsätze
summary: Relative clauses with der/die/das add detail about a noun.
explanation:
A Relativsatz describes a noun using a relative pronoun (der, die, das, plural die) that matches the noun's gender/number but takes its case from its own role inside the clause. Like other subordinate clauses, the verb goes to the end.

The relative pronoun looks like the definite article but changes for case: nominative der/die/das/die, accusative den/die/das/die, dative dem/der/dem/denen. A comma always separates the Relativsatz from the rest of the sentence.

examples.de: Der Mann, der dort steht, ist mein Chef.
examples.en: The man who is standing there is my boss.

examples.de: Das Buch, das ich lese, ist spannend.
examples.en: The book (that) I'm reading is exciting.

examples.de: Die Frau, der ich geholfen habe, heißt Anna.
examples.en: The woman (whom) I helped is called Anna.

examples.de: Das ist der Film, den ich letzte Woche gesehen habe.
examples.en: That's the film (that) I saw last week.

tips: First decide the noun's gender (fixes the row), then decide the pronoun's own case from its job inside the Relativsatz (fixes the column).
Unlike English, German never drops the relative pronoun — 'the book I read' still needs das.

title: Komparativ und Superlativ
summary: Comparing adjectives: -er for more, am -sten for most.
explanation:
The Komparativ (comparative) adds -er to the adjective, and the Superlativ (superlative) uses am + adjective + -sten. Many short, common adjectives with a, o, or u also add an Umlaut in both forms.

Use als after a comparative to mean 'than', and (genau)so … wie for 'as … as'. A handful of adjectives are irregular and must be memorized, similar to English good/better/best.

examples.de: Der Zug ist schneller als das Auto.
examples.en: The train is faster than the car.

examples.de: Mein Bruder ist so groß wie ich.
examples.en: My brother is as tall as I am.

examples.de: Berlin ist die größte Stadt in Deutschland.
examples.en: Berlin is the biggest city in Germany.
I like eating pizza the most.

tips: als = 'than' after a comparative; wie = 'as' after so...
gut/besser/am besten and viel/mehr/am meisten don't follow the -er/-sten pattern — learn them as a pair like English.

title: Wechselpräpositionen
summary: Nine prepositions that take Akkusativ for movement, Dativ for location.
explanation:
Nine prepositions (an, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor, zwischen) switch case depending on meaning: Akkusativ answers wohin? (movement toward a destination — 'where to'), Dativ answers wo? (static location — 'where at').

The test is whether the verb describes a change of place (movement into/onto/behind something) or a state of being in a place. Verbs like stellen/legen/hängen (put) usually pair with Akkusativ; stehen/liegen/hängen (be positioned) usually pair with Dativ.

tables.caption: wohin? (Akkusativ) vs. wo? (Dativ)
rows: Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch.
Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.

examples.de: Ich stelle die Vase auf den Tisch.
examples.en: I put the vase on the table. (movement)

examples.de: Die Vase steht auf dem Tisch.
examples.en: The vase is (standing) on the table. (location)

tips: Ask wohin? or wo? first — the answer picks the case, not the preposition itself.
in + das contracts to ins, in + dem to im, an + das to ans, an + dem to am.

title: Reflexive Verben
summary: Verbs whose action reflects back onto the subject, with sich.
explanation:
Reflexive verbs pair a verb with a reflexive pronoun (mich, dich, sich, uns, euch, sich) that refers back to the subject. Most reflexive pronouns are Akkusativ, but a few verbs take a Dativ reflexive pronoun when there's also a direct object.

Some verbs are always reflexive (sich freuen — to be happy), while others are only reflexive in certain meanings (sich waschen — to wash oneself, vs. waschen — to wash something else).

examples.de: Ich freue mich auf das Wochenende.
examples.en: I'm looking forward to the weekend.

examples.de: Wir treffen uns um acht Uhr.
examples.en: We're meeting (each other) at eight o'clock.
I brush my teeth. (Dativ mir — die Zähne is the object)

tips: Only sich changes to mir/dir when the sentence already has a direct object (die Zähne) — the reflexive pronoun then takes the leftover Dativ slot.
Look up new verbs with sich in the dictionary form to know they're reflexive.

title: Modalverben im Präteritum
summary: Past tense of können, müssen, wollen, dürfen, sollen, mögen.
explanation:
Modal verbs almost always use Präteritum for the past, even in speech, because their forms are short and natural. Like other Präteritum verbs, they lose their Umlaut (können → konnte, müssen → musste, dürfen → durfte) and take the same personal endings as regular Präteritum verbs.

A modal verb's Präteritum still pairs with a second verb in the infinitive at the end of the clause, exactly like the Präsens does.

examples.en: We had to take the bus.
He wanted to become a doctor.

examples.de: Durftet ihr als Kinder lange fernsehen?
examples.en: Were you allowed to watch TV a lot as children?

tips: ich and er/sie/es share the same Präteritum form for modals, with no extra ending — unlike Präsens.
The Umlaut disappears in the Präteritum: können→konnte, müssen→musste, dürfen→durfte.

title: Possessivartikel im Dativ
summary: Possessives (mein, dein, sein...) declined for the dative case.
explanation:
Possessivartikel take the same endings as ein/kein, but in the Dativ every gender gets an -em/-er ending: dative masculine and neuter add -em, feminine adds -er, and plural adds -en (on every possessive, regardless of gender).

The possessive still agrees with the noun it describes, not with the owner — mein Vater but meiner Mutter, because Vater is masculine and Mutter is feminine.

examples.en: We live at our grandparents' place.

examples.de: Er schreibt seiner Freundin einen Brief.
examples.en: He writes his girlfriend a letter.

tips: In the Dativ, the ending depends only on the noun's gender/number, not on who owns it.
Plural Dativ nouns also add -n to the noun itself if it doesn't already end in -n or -s (den Freunden).

title: Genitiv — Grundlagen
summary: The possessive case: des/der + noun, masculine/neuter nouns add -s.
explanation:
The Genitiv expresses possession ('the car of the man' / 'the man's car') and appears after certain prepositions (wegen, trotz, während, außerhalb). In everyday speech it's often replaced by von + Dativ, but it's still expected in writing and on exams.

Masculine and neuter nouns in the Genitiv add -(e)s to the noun itself, on top of the article changing to des; feminine and plural nouns only change the article, to der.

examples.de: Das ist das Haus meiner Eltern.
Wegen des Wetters bleiben wir zu Hause.
examples.en: Because of the weather we're staying home.

examples.de: Der Titel des Buches gefällt mir.
examples.en: I like the title of the book.

examples.de: Trotz des Regens gehen wir spazieren.
examples.en: Despite the rain we're going for a walk.

tips: In spoken German, 'von + Dativ' (die Tasche von der Frau) is very common instead of the Genitiv — but recognize and use the Genitiv for writing/exams.
One-syllable masculine/neuter nouns usually add -es (des Mannes), longer ones just -s (des Autos).

title: Passiv Präsens
summary: The passive voice: werden + Partizip II shifts focus from doer to action.
explanation:
The Passiv puts the focus on the action or the thing affected rather than who does it: 'the door is opened' instead of 'someone opens the door'. It's formed with a conjugated form of werden plus the Partizip II of the main verb at the end of the clause.

If the doer still needs to be named, use von + Dativ (for a person/agent) or durch + Akkusativ (for a cause/means). Often the doer is simply left out because it's unknown or unimportant.

examples.de: Das Restaurant wird jeden Abend geöffnet.
examples.en: The restaurant is opened every evening.

examples.de: Die E-Mail wird von der Chefin geschrieben.
examples.en: The email is written by the boss.

examples.de: Der Brief wird durch die Post zugestellt.
examples.en: The letter is delivered by the postal service.

tips: Don't confuse Passiv-werden with sein + adjective — 'die Tür wird geöffnet' (process) vs. 'die Tür ist geöffnet' (resulting state, Zustandspassiv).
The doer (if named) uses von for a person, durch for a cause or means.

title: Indirekte Fragen
summary: Embedding a question inside a sentence: verb moves to the end.
explanation:
An indirekte Frage embeds a question inside a larger, more polite sentence ('I'd like to know whether...' instead of 'Do you...?'). Like other subordinate clauses, the verb goes to the end.

W-questions (wann, wo, was, warum, wie…) keep their question word as the connector. Yes/no questions use ob ('whether/if') as the connector instead, since there's no question word to reuse.

tables.caption: Direct vs. indirect question
rows: Ich weiß nicht, wann der Bus kommt.
Können Sie mir sagen, wo Sie wohnen?
Ich frage mich, ob du mitkommst.
Ich weiß nicht, ob er angerufen hat.

examples.de: Ich weiß nicht, wie viel das kostet.
examples.en: I don't know how much that costs.

examples.de: Können Sie mir sagen, ob der Zug pünktlich ist?
examples.en: Can you tell me whether the train is on time?

examples.de: Er fragt, warum ich so spät komme.
examples.en: He's asking why I'm coming so late.

examples.de: Weißt du, wo der Bahnhof ist?
examples.en: Do you know where the train station is?

tips: No question mark and no verb-second at the start — it's a statement containing a question, so the connector word sends the verb to the end.
Use ob only when the direct question has no question word (yes/no questions).

title: Infinitiv mit zu
summary: zu + infinitive after certain verbs, adjectives, and expressions.
explanation:
After many verbs (versuchen, hoffen, vergessen, planen…), adjectives (wichtig, schwer, einfach) and expressions like Es macht Spaß, a second verb appears as zu + infinitive at the end of the clause — with a comma before it if the phrase has more than one part.

Separable verbs insert zu between the prefix and the stem, written as one word: aufzustehen, einzukaufen. Modal verbs and a few others (gehen, lassen, sehen, hören) never take zu.

tables.caption: zu-Infinitiv patterns
rows: Es ist wichtig, Deutsch zu lernen.
Ich lerne Deutsch, um in Deutschland zu arbeiten.

examples.de: Es macht Spaß, Deutsch zu lernen.
Sie hofft, den Job zu bekommen.
examples.en: She hopes to get the job.
We're going shopping. (gehen never takes zu)

tips: For separable verbs, zu slots inside the word: auf + zu + stehen → aufzustehen.
um...zu expresses purpose ('in order to'); plain zu just links two verbs.

title: je … desto
summary: Correlative comparatives: 'the more..., the more...'.
explanation:
je … desto links two comparatives to show that one thing changes in proportion to another, like English 'the more..., the more...'. Both clauses use a comparative adjective/adverb right after je and desto.

The je-clause is a Nebensatz, so its verb goes to the end; the desto-clause is a special main clause where desto + comparative comes first and is immediately followed by the verb (verb-second still applies to the whole desto-clause).

examples.de: Je mehr ich übe, desto besser werde ich.
examples.en: The more I practice, the better I get.

examples.de: Je älter er wird, desto ruhiger wird er.
examples.en: The older he gets, the calmer he becomes.

examples.de: Je früher wir losfahren, desto weniger Verkehr gibt es.
examples.en: The earlier we leave, the less traffic there is.

examples.de: Je größer die Stadt, desto teurer die Miete.
examples.en: The bigger the city, the more expensive the rent.

tips: The je-clause always sends its verb to the end (it's a Nebensatz); the desto-clause keeps verb-second right after desto + comparative.
Both comparatives can be adjectives or adverbs, but the je...desto skeleton never changes.
